tracks.title: Toledo in five minutes: the city on the rock

sections.title: The city that translated the world

segments.text: Welcome to Toledo, Monica.
Before any church or painting, here is the story of the city itself.
It takes five minutes, and everything else today will make more sense.
Start with the ground under your feet.
Toledo sits on a hill of granite, and the river Tagus wraps around it on three sides, in a deep gorge.
Only one side is open.
Whoever held this rock was very hard to remove.
So everyone wanted it.
The Romans took it first, about two hundred years before Christ.
One of their historians called it a small city, but strong because of its position.
They built baths, a circus for chariot races, and the water tanks you can still visit underground.
When Rome collapsed, a people from the north moved in.
The Visigoths.
They made Toledo the capital of all Spain.
Their kings were crowned here, and their bishops met here to decide what the country would believe.
Remember them.
Their last king, Rodrigo, is waiting for you in tonight's legends.
Then, in seven hundred and eleven, an army crossed from Africa.
Within a few years, Toledo was a Muslim city, and it stayed one for nearly four hundred years.
The narrow twisting lanes you keep getting lost in are their street plan.
The little mosque by the city gate is theirs.
You have just come from Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain.
Granada fell in fourteen ninety-two.
Toledo was taken by a Christian king four centuries earlier, in ten eighty-five.
It was the first great Muslim city to fall.
And that is the reason it matters so much.
Because the new Christian king did something unusual.
He did not empty the city.
Muslims stayed.
Jews stayed.
And so did their libraries.
Those libraries held books Europe had lost.
Greek medicine, astronomy, mathematics, Aristotle.
All of it kept alive in Arabic.
So scholars came to Toledo from England, Italy and Germany, and sat down with Jewish and Muslim translators.
A book would go from Arabic into Spanish, spoken aloud, and from Spanish into Latin, written down.
Think about that, with your own story.
Knowledge passing from one language to the next, across a table, between people who prayed differently.
Much of what Europe later called its Renaissance came through rooms in this town.
It was not paradise.
There were taxes, quarrels, and massacres.
But for a few centuries, three faiths shared this small rock, and built in each other's styles.
You will see churches that look like mosques, built by Muslim craftsmen for Christian priests.
It ended badly.
In fourteen ninety-two, the Jews of Spain were told to convert or leave.
Ten years later, the Muslims were told the same.
The city of three faiths became a city of one.
For a while Toledo was still the heart of an empire.
The emperor Charles the Fifth, the one you saw on horseback in the Prado, held court here.
Then his son moved the capital to a small town in the middle of nowhere, called Madrid.
The court left.
The money left.
And Toledo simply stopped.
Nobody could afford to knock it down and build it again.
That is why you are walking through a medieval city today.
It was preserved by being forgotten.
One man arrived a few years after the court had gone.
A painter from Greece, hoping to work for the king.
The king tried him once, and did not like the result.
So he stayed here for the rest of his life, and painted this city's priests, its noblemen and its stormy sky.
You know him already.
El Greco.
That is Toledo.
Romans, Goths, Muslims, Christians and Jews, all on one rock, and then four centuries of sleep.
Now choose your next track.
The cathedral, Santo Tomé, or whatever is in front of you.

tracks.title: Stop 1. Santo Tomé: The Burial of the Count of Orgaz

sections.title: A debt two hundred years old

segments.text: Stop one.
The church of Santo Tomé, with its brick tower.
The painting has its own entrance beside the church; check at the door.
Go in and stand back from it.
It fills the wall.
This picture starts with money.
A rich nobleman of Toledo, the lord of the town of Orgaz, loved this little parish church.
When he died, in thirteen twenty-three, he left it a gift to be paid every year, from Orgaz, for ever.
For ever lasted about two centuries.
Then the payments stopped.
The parish priest of Santo Tomé, Andrés Núñez, went to law.
He won.
And then he did something clever.
He decided the whole city should see, every day, why that money was owed.
He would put the nobleman's funeral on the wall, miracle and all.
So he hired the foreigner Toledo was talking about.
A painter from Crete.
They called him the Greek.
El Greco.
Here is the legend, as Toledo tells it.
At the funeral, as the body was about to be lowered, two saints came down from heaven.
Saint Stephen, young.
Saint Augustine, old and bearded.
They lifted the dead man with their own hands and laid him in his tomb, while the mourners stared.
That is legend.
The contract spelled it out: the miracle, the saints, and the crowd who saw it.
The painter would pay for his own materials.
The price would be set by valuers when it was done.
Look at the bottom half.
The two saints in gold, bending under the weight of a body in black armour.
How gently they hold him.
The old saint cradles his shoulders.
The young one holds his legs.
Now look closely at the young saint's robe, low down near his hem.
There is a tiny picture painted on it.
A man being stoned.
That is Stephen's own death, the first Christian martyr, embroidered on the clothes he wears to bury someone else.
Look at the row of men behind.
Black clothes.
White ruffs.
Long pale faces.
They look like portraits because many of them were.
Gentlemen of Toledo in El Greco's own day, not the dead man's.
The painter put his neighbours at a funeral two hundred and sixty years old.
On the right, in a white robe, reading from a book, is the priest who won the lawsuit.
Núñez put himself at the funeral he had fought for.
Now look above the row of faces, a little left of centre.
Find a knight with a red cross on his chest, his hand raised.
Just above that hand, one man is not watching the miracle.
He is looking straight at you.
He is said to be El Greco himself.
Now the lower left corner.
A small boy in black, holding a torch.
He points at the saints, and looks out at you.
This is the painter's son, Jorge Manuel.
Look at the white handkerchief in his pocket.
On it El Greco wrote his own name, and the year fifteen seventy-eight.
Not the year of the painting.
The year the boy was born.
El Greco probably never married the boy's mother.
But he signed his greatest picture on his son, and put the child at the front, where no one could miss him.
Lift your eyes.
Up the middle, an angel carries something small and pale, like a newborn baby.
It is the dead man's soul, squeezed upward through a narrow passage of cloud.
Look among the blessed at the top for faces in black.
El Greco even placed the living king of Spain up there.
When it was finished, the valuers named a price.
The parish thought it far too much.
Arguments, appeals, lawyers.
In the end El Greco gave in and accepted the lower valuation, and part of it was paid off against debts he owed.
That was his life in Toledo.
He rented a huge set of rooms in an old palace by the Jewish quarter, more than twenty of them.
He lived grandly.
It is said he sometimes had musicians play while he dined.
And he was always in court, suing patrons who would not pay.
One more glimpse of him.
When a fellow Greek was brought before the Inquisition in Toledo, El Greco was called in to interpret.
A foreigner himself, translating for one of his own, before the most feared court in Spain.
He died in Toledo, still working, with debts unpaid.
On his deathbed he gave his son the power to write his will.
Look back at the boy one last time.
Four hundred years on, he is still pointing, still asking you to look.
Walk on, down the hill, to the great stone monastery with chains on its walls.
That is stop two, San Juan de los Reyes.

tracks.room: Church of Santo Tomé, Calle Santo Tomé

tracks.title: Stop 2. San Juan de los Reyes: A tomb left empty

segments.text: Stop two.
The monastery of San Juan de los Reyes.
Before you go in, stay outside.
Find the long wall of pale stone facing the street, and look up.
Iron chains, hanging in loops high on the stone.
Shackles.
Manacles.
From the street they look like decoration.
They are not.
These chains were worn by Christian prisoners held in the Muslim kingdom of Granada.
As the armies of Isabella and Ferdinand took its towns, one by one, the captives were set free, and their chains were sent here and hung on the wall of the queen's church.
Which prisons, exactly?
The stories differ.
Some say Granada itself.
Others name Málaga, or Ronda, or towns further east.
What they agree on is the message.
Look what we did.
We brought our people home.
You have just come from Granada.
Picture a man stepping out of a cell there, into the light, rubbing his wrists.
His chains ended up here, as a trophy.
Now hold a question as you go in.
Why build a church this grand, and then not use it for the one thing it was made for?
Go back to the beginning.
When Isabella claimed the crown of Castile, her claim was not safe.
Her niece said the crown was hers, and the king of Portugal married that niece and marched into Castile to take it.
In fourteen seventy-six the two armies met near a town called Toro, on the river Duero.
The fighting went on into the dark.
On one side of the field the Portuguese did well.
On the other, Ferdinand's men broke them.
Both sides claimed the victory.
But Isabella understood something.
A battle is won by whoever tells the story.
She called it a triumph, gave thanks, and vowed a monastery.
Here, in Toledo, the old heart of Castile.
And it would be their tomb.
The architect was Juan Guas, the queen's master of works.
Now a story Toledo loves to tell.
The queen came to see how her church was going.
She looked around and asked whether this trifle was what they had built her.
In old Spanish, "esta nonada".
A nothing.
It is a story, and the words differ from one telling to the next.
But the building did change.
It grew richer, and grander, to match her vow.
Walk up to the crossing, where the great stone arches meet.
Look at the walls.
They are covered in coats of arms, held up by huge stone eagles.
The eagle is the sign of Saint John, whose church this is.
Now look for two small emblems, again and again.
A yoke, the wooden collar for oxen.
And a bundle of arrows.
The yoke was Ferdinand's sign.
The arrows were Isabella's.
The popular story says each picked the other's initial.
Yugo, yoke, with a Y, the old spelling of Isabel.
Flechas, arrows, with an F, for Fernando.
Whether or not that is why they chose them, look how they are carved here.
Side by side, again and again, like lovers' initials on a tree.
So why are they not here?
Because of Granada.
In fourteen ninety-two the last Muslim kingdom in Spain surrendered, and the Alhambra was theirs.
The queen loved that city.
She decided to be buried there instead, in the place of her greatest victory.
When she died, her body was carried south and laid first in a convent inside the Alhambra itself.
If you walked past the Parador hotel up there, that old convent is where she first lay.
Later she and Ferdinand were moved to the Royal Chapel, beside Granada's cathedral.
They are there still.
This church was left without its king and queen.
A tomb with nobody in it.
Before you leave, walk into the cloister.
Two floors of arches around a garden.
Look up at the carving, at the beasts and odd creatures sticking out from the walls.
In eighteen hundred and eight, Napoleon's troops occupied Toledo and were quartered here.
A great fire broke out.
The second cloister was destroyed altogether.
Much of what you see was rebuilt later, by restorers working from what survived.
One wing of this cloister and the lace of stone along its top are largely theirs.
So look closely.
Some faces up there were carved five centuries ago.
Some, little more than one.
See if you can tell which.
Stand in the garden.
Think of that wall outside.
The chains of men set free, hung on a church built for a queen who chose to lie somewhere else.
Walk on, uphill, across the old town, to the little mosque of Cristo de la Luz.
That is stop three.

tracks.room: Jewish quarter, Calle de los Reyes Católicos

tracks.title: Stop 3. Cristo de la Luz: The mosque by daylight

segments.text: Stop three.
The little mosque of Cristo de la Luz, near the Sun Gate.
You know its legend already, the king's horse that knelt in the street, and the lamp still burning behind the wall.
Now see the building by daylight.
Start outside, on the street side.
Find the front wall of narrow red bricks, with its three arched doorways.
Above them, blind arches cross and weave like basketwork.
Now look along the very top, just under the roof line.
A band of brick letters runs across it.
That is Arabic, in an old, square, angular script.
And it is a signature.
It says, in short, that a man named Ahmad ibn Hadidi had this mosque built, hoping for his reward from God.
That it was finished, with God's help, under the direction of a builder, Musa ibn Ali, and a man called Saada.
And it gives the date.
The year Christians count as nine hundred and ninety-nine.
Think about that.
One man's money.
One builder's skill.
A small neighbourhood mosque, at the end of the first millennium.
Toledo had many like it.
Almost all are gone.
This is the one that survived, and it still carries the name of the man who made it.
Now go inside.
It is tiny.
Four columns hold up the whole roof.
Stand in the middle, between them.
Look at the tops of the columns, the capitals.
They do not match, and they are rougher than the walls around them.
That is because the builder did not carve them.
He reused them.
They came from older buildings, from the Christian Visigoths who ruled Toledo before the Muslims came.
One was remade in a restoration a century ago.
So the oldest stones holding up this mosque were carved by Christians, and they would hold it up again when it became a church.
Now look up.
The ceiling is divided into nine little squares, three by three.
Each one has its own small dome.
And each dome is made differently.
Brick ribs crossing in a new pattern every time.
Stars.
Crosses.
Grids.
Turn slowly and look at all nine.
It is a builder showing off nine ways to make a sky.
If you saw the great mosque of Córdoba, you will know this family of ribbed domes from the dome in front of its prayer niche.
This is its small country cousin.
Now look east, to the far end.
The style changes.
A rounded apse, a half-circle chamber, joined on in the same red brick, but later.
After the Christian conquest, the mosque passed to a crusading order, the Knights of Saint John, and about two centuries after it was built, they added this apse.
Christian prayer had to face east, so the church grew a new head.
Look into the curved vault of the apse.
Faded paintings, patchy.
At the centre was Christ in majesty, seated in glory.
Much of it has flaked away.
Look for an outline, a hand, a halo.
One building, joined at the seam.
Muslim domes on one side.
Christian saints on the other.
One last thing, outside again.
This hill was a Roman town before it was anything else.
About twenty years ago, archaeologists digging beside the mosque uncovered a stretch of Roman street.
Big granite paving slabs, a road about five metres wide, with a drain running underneath.
Look in the garden area next to the building for the opened ground.
Sources disagree on exactly where it shows, so if you cannot see it, check at the door.
Picture carts rolling over those slabs, nearly a thousand years before the bricks went up.
So stand here for a moment.
Roman stones in the ground.
Visigothic capitals in the columns.
A Muslim builder's name above the door.
Christian saints at the end.
All of Toledo, in a room you could cross in ten steps.
Walk on, through the old streets, to the church of San Román.
That is stop four.

tracks.room: Near Puerta del Sol, Calle Cristo de la Luz

tracks.title: Stop 4. San Román: Arabic on a Christian wall

sections.title: A church that speaks two languages
The victory painted on the walls
The boy king in the tower

segments.text: Stop four.
The church of San Román, on the high ground at the centre of the old town.
These days it is the Museum of the Councils and Visigothic Culture.
Go in, stand in the middle of the nave, and look at the arches first.
Horseshoe arches, in rows, like the ones you just saw at the little mosque.
Now look at the columns holding them up.
They do not match.
Some are older than the church by many centuries, taken from Visigothic and even Roman buildings and set up again here.
But this was never a mosque.
It was built as a church, by Christians, in the Mudéjar way: the building style of Muslim craftsmen, working for Christian patrons.
Hold a question.
Why would a Christian archbishop want Arabic letters in his church?
Here is the scene.
Early in the thirteenth century, a Christian army has just crushed a Muslim army in the south, at a place called Las Navas de Tolosa.
The Archbishop of Toledo rode with that army.
Back home, he has this church painted and consecrated again, to celebrate.
Now look up at the walls.
The paintings are in two bands, one above the other, with a strip of lettering running between them.
Look for the four evangelists, each with wings.
Look for a row of bishops, the archbishops of Toledo.
Look for two young saints in deacon's robes, Stephen and Lawrence.
And look around the arches for more bands of writing.
Some of it is Latin, in verse.
Some of it is in Arabic letters.
One answer to the question: in Toledo, Arabic was not only the enemy's script.
It was the look of beauty and learning, the way fine buildings were dressed.
So a victory over the Muslim south was painted in a style that came from it.
Scholars still argue over what some of that Arabic says, and whether it was meant to be read at all.
Perhaps it was there simply to look splendid.
Now find the Last Judgement.
In Christian belief it is the day the dead rise from their graves to be judged.
See if you can find them, small figures rising to face their judge.
In a church built to give thanks for a battle, the painters put the end of the world.
Everyone, winner and loser, will answer in the end.
Before you go further, a story about the tower outside.
Toledo tells that in a time of civil war, when the city was held by rivals, a child king of Castile was brought in by surprise, and shown to the people from the tower of San Román.
The city rose for him, and his enemies fled.
That boy grew up to be the king who won at Las Navas.
The details vary from one teller to the next.
But it is a good tale to have in your head when you look up at that tower.
Now walk round the cases.
Before the Muslims came, Toledo was the capital of the Visigoths, a Germanic people who ruled Spain from here for well over a century.
Their bishops met in great councils in this city, and at one of them a king gave up his old faith and took the Catholic one.
That is why the museum carries the councils' name.
Look for the belt buckles, the jewellery, the carved stones.
And look for the copies of the gold crowns of Guarrazar.
Check at the door if you cannot find them.
The story goes that one summer in the eighteen fifties, after heavy rain near a village outside Toledo, a farming couple found gold glinting in the earth.
It was a buried hoard of crowns and crosses, hidden, it is thought, when the Muslims arrived.
Pieces were sold off quietly, some to France.
The originals are now in Madrid and Paris.
Kings hung them over altars as gifts to God.
On the finest, gold letters hang from the rim, spelling out a king's name and the words "offers this".
If the copies here include it, find those letters.
One crown, of another king, was stolen from the royal armoury in Madrid in the twentieth century.
It has never been found.
Stand under the arches once more.
Roman columns.
Visigothic gold.
Arabic letters.
Christian saints, and the Last Judgement.
One small church, holding every Toledo at once.
Walk on, downhill, to the cathedral.
That is stop five.

tracks.room: Museum of the Councils and Visigothic Culture, Calle San Román

tracks.title: Stop 5. The Cathedral: Six things not to miss

sections.title: One. A hole in the roof
Five. The room of the archbishops

segments.text: Stop five.
The cathedral of Toledo.
Six things, six stories, in any order.
Pause between them, find the next one, and press play.
This was the seat of the most powerful churchman in Spain, the Archbishop of Toledo.
Everything here was made by people with money, who wanted to be seen spending it on God.
Walk round behind the high altar, into the passage at the back.
Stop when the light changes.
Then turn, and look up.
Marble clouds.
Angels tumbling.
Rays of gold.
And above it all, real daylight, pouring through a hole in the ceiling.
This is the Transparente.
Behind the high altar the bread of the Mass was kept, the most holy thing in the church.
But it sat in the dark.
So, in the seventeen hundreds, a sculptor named Narciso Tomé did something outrageous.
He cut a hole in the Gothic vault of this cathedral and let the sun in.
Some people at the time were thrilled.
Some were horrified.
Which are you?
Find the Last Supper, carved high up in the marble, and watch how the light lands on it.
Now go to the sacristy.
Walk to the far end of the long room.
The painting on the end wall.
El Greco's Disrobing of Christ.
One of his first commissions in Toledo.
If you saw his saints at the Prado, this is where his Spanish story starts.
Look at the robe.
That red.
It burns out of a crowd of grey faces and steel.
Christ looks up.
The soldiers close in.
Someone is already reaching for the cloth.
The cathedral did not like it.
They argued about the price, and it went to valuation.
And, as the story goes, they objected to the three Marys in the corner, who are not in the Gospel at this moment.
Look at the three women, lower left.
They stayed.
A young foreigner, fighting the richest church in Spain.
The picture has hung here ever since.
Now walk to the choir, the enclosed space in the middle of the nave.
Look at the lower row of wooden seats, and above each seat, the carved panel.
Every panel is a scene from one war.
The conquest of Granada.
Towns falling.
Walls.
Ladders.
Turbaned defenders on the battlements.
Knights with banners riding in.
A carver named Rodrigo Alemán made them, only a few years after the war ended.
More than fifty scenes.
The war was still news.
You have just walked through the Alhambra, the prize at the end of this war.
Find one panel and look at the people on the walls.
Someone is about to lose their city.
Now find the Treasury chapel.
Behind the glass, a tower taller than a person, in silver and gold.
The great monstrance, the Custodia.
It was made to carry the holy bread through the streets at Corpus Christi, and still goes out each year.
Look into its heart.
At the centre there is a smaller piece, in gold.
That one belonged to Queen Isabella.
After her death, the cathedral acquired it, and the goldsmith built this great tower around it.
The guides love a story.
The gilding, they say, was done with the first gold Columbus brought back from the Americas.
Nobody has proved it.
But look at the shine, and think of where gold came from in those years.
Now find the Chapter House, off the walkway behind the high altar.
The room where the canons met to govern.
Look up first.
A ceiling of carved and painted wood, gold and colour, in the Mudéjar style.
Then the walls, painted all over by Juan de Borgoña.
Scenes from the life of the Virgin.
And at the far end, the Last Judgement.
A message for the men who sat here: you will answer for what you decide in this room.
Now look lower, along the walls, under the frescoes.
A long row of painted faces.
These are the archbishops of Toledo, one after another, reaching back toward the earliest centuries.
The early faces are imagined; there was nothing to copy.
The man who built this room was Cardinal Cisneros, archbishop, regent of Spain, the queen's confessor.
A row of predecessors around the room where he ruled.
He was telling everyone who walked in that he stood at the end of a line more than a thousand years long.
Last, find the Mozarabic Chapel, near the main west doors.
It may be closed outside its service; check at the door.
When Toledo was a Muslim city, its Christians kept their own old way of worship, different from Rome's.
They were called Mozarabs.
When Christian kings took Toledo, the new rulers wanted the Roman way instead.
Now the legend.
The king, they say, ordered a trial by fire.
Two prayer books were thrown into the flames, the Roman and the Toledan.
The Toledan book would not burn.
And so the old rite was allowed to survive.
That is legend.
What is true is this.
Cardinal Cisneros, the man of the Chapter House, founded this chapel to keep the old rite alive.
It is still celebrated here.
Of all the gold in this building, that may be the rarest thing.
A way of praying older than the cathedral, still spoken inside it.
When you are ready, the closing track is stop six.
Play it wherever you are.

tracks.room: Cathedral of Toledo, Plaza del Ayuntamiento

tracks.title: Stop 6. Toledo: The city of three cultures

segments.text: Stop six, the last.
Play this wherever you are.
If you can, find a spot where you can see the river bending round the rock.
You will hear it everywhere in Toledo.
The city of three cultures.
Christians, Muslims and Jews, side by side.
It is on the posters and in the shops.
Is it true?
The honest answer is yes, and no.
Think of what you saw today.
A mosque whose builder signed his name in brick.
A church with Arabic letters round its arches.
And in the Jewish quarter you walked through, two synagogues still stand, one built by Muslim craftsmen, one decorated like a palace of Granada.
In this city, scholars of three faiths worked together, turning books from Arabic into Latin and Castilian.
Astronomy, medicine, philosophy, much of it Greek learning kept alive in Arabic, came back into Europe through Toledo.
That was real.
It made this city.
But living side by side is not the same as being equal.
Jews and Muslims lived under Christian law, protected in good times, and in bad times by nobody.
In thirteen ninety-one, riots swept the Jewish quarters of Castile.
Synagogues were taken.
Then, fourteen ninety-two.
The year Granada fell.
That spring, Isabella and Ferdinand signed the order expelling every Jew who would not convert.
They signed it in the Alhambra.
The palace you walked through.
Families who had lived here longer than anyone could remember had a few months to go.
Many left, for Portugal, North Africa, the lands of the Ottomans.
Their descendants kept speaking a form of Spanish for five hundred years.
The Muslims of Castile were forced to convert a few years later, and a century after that, their descendants were expelled too.
Some Sephardic families are said to have carried the keys of their Spanish houses with them, and kept them for generations.
It is hard to prove.
The story has never died.
So the three cultures are here, in the stone.
The people who made it are mostly gone.
The beauty is real.
The loss is real.
Toledo asks you to carry both.
Look at the river one last time, wrapped round the city like an arm.
Thank you for walking it with me, Monica.
Take the train back to Madrid.
And if you go back to the Prado, find El Greco again.
You have stood in his city now, in front of his son.
His saints will look different.
Goodbye, Toledo.

tracks.room: Anywhere, ideally a viewpoint over the river

tracks.title: Toledo after dark: the legends

sections.title: A city that keeps its secrets

segments.text: Good evening, Monica.
The sun has gone down behind the river, the day crowds have gone home, and Toledo is starting to change.
You have seen this city by daylight.
Churches, synagogues, a cathedral, the old mosque.
Christians, Jews and Muslims, living side by side on one rock above the Tagus for centuries.
Tonight is for the other Toledo.
The one that people whisper about.
For hundreds of years, all over Europe, this city's name meant magic.
Students were said to come here to learn to raise the dead.
Kings were said to lose their kingdoms here by opening the wrong door.
Statues here move.
Crucifixes speak.
A wooden man once walked these streets.
Why here?
Think about where you are standing.
A maze of lanes too narrow for the moon.
Three faiths, each with its own scholars and its own secrets.
Libraries full of books in languages most of Europe could not read.
A city like that breeds stories after dark.
The Spanish have a phrase for a night when nobody sleeps.
Una noche toledana.
A Toledan night.
One story behind the phrase is the darkest in the city.
Listen.
More than a thousand years ago, Toledo kept rebelling against the emir in far-off Córdoba.
So the emir sent a new governor, a man named Amrus.
He announced a great feast to welcome the prince, and invited the leading men of Toledo to his palace.
They came in, one by one, through a single gate.
And one by one, as they entered, they were killed.
Their bodies went into a pit dug in secret.
Hundreds of them.
Toledo did not sleep that night.
And it did not rebel again for a long time.
Arab chroniclers tell this massacre as history, and some scholars doubt it.
And the phrase may come from something smaller.
An old dictionary from four centuries ago blamed it on the mosquitoes, which ate visitors alive in the summer heat.
At seven, you join the legends tour.
It will be in Spanish.
Each track here tells you one story in English, before you get there.
Listen over a drink, or standing at the place itself.
Then, when the guide stops, drops their voice and points, you will know exactly what they are pointing at.
You will know when the horse kneels, and when the statue moves.
One promise.
When I tell you a legend, you will hear it in another voice.
When I tell you what really happened, it will be me.
Keep them apart, and enjoy both.
Some of the places are shut at night, and you will only see their doors and walls.
That is how legends should be met.
From outside, in the dark.
Start with the little mosque by the old gate, and a horse that would not take another step.
That is stop one.

tracks.room: Anywhere in the old town, before the tour

tracks.title: Stop 1. Cristo de la Luz: the horse that knelt

sections.title: The horse that would not move

segments.text: Stop one.
The small brick mosque of Cristo de la Luz stands on a steep lane just inside the old walls, near the Puerta del Sol gate.
It closes before dark, so tonight you will see it from outside: a little square building of red brick, with arches over arches in its walls.
It is older than almost anything around you.
An inscription on its front gives the year it was finished, nine hundred and ninety-nine.
A thousand years ago, this was a neighbourhood mosque.
Now the story.
Picture a spring day, almost a century later.
Toledo has opened its gates to a Christian king.
King Alfonso rides in at the head of his army, in triumph, up this very slope.
Beside him rides his greatest knight, they say, the Cid.
And then, here, outside this little mosque, the king's horse stops.
It will not go on.
The king spurs it.
Nothing.
And then, in front of the whole army, the horse slowly bends its front legs, and kneels in the street.
Facing the wall of the mosque.
Why would a horse kneel to a wall?
Hold that question.
The king orders the wall opened.
The soldiers strike at the stones.
And behind them they find a hollow, a hidden niche.
Inside it, a crucifix.
And beside the crucifix, an oil lamp.
Still burning.
Here is the secret, as the legend tells it.
Nearly four hundred years before, when the Muslim armies came, the Christians of Toledo hid their Christ in this wall to save it, and lit a lamp beside it.
They sealed it up.
They died.
Nobody remembered.
And all that time, in the dark, the little flame kept burning.
Waiting for someone to come back for it.
That is why the building is called Christ of the Light.
And they say the king held the first Christian Mass here, and left his shield behind, with a cross on it, hanging in the church.
Now the history.
The king was real, and he did take Toledo in ten eighty-five.
The mosque really did become a chapel.
But the legend appears only after the conquest, told by the winners.
Some tellings even forget the lamp.
Others put the Cid on the horse.
The kneeling horse belongs to the story, not the record.
When you are outside, look down at the paving in front of the building.
Toledans say one white stone marks the spot where the horse went down on its knees.
Look for it with the guide's torch.
And stand a moment with this.
The lamp of the legend burned for a faith that was hidden.
The building that kept it was built by another faith.
Whose light is it?
Next, down under the streets near the cathedral, to a palace no king was ever meant to open.
That is stop two.

tracks.room: Mosque of Cristo de la Luz, near the Puerta del Sol gate, north side of the old town

tracks.title: Stop 2. The Cave of Hercules: the king who broke the locks

segments.text: Stop two.
The Cave of Hercules is under a narrow alley called Callejón de San Ginés, a short walk from the cathedral.
It opens only for a few hours in the daytime, so tonight you will stand at a plain door in the alley and look down, in your mind, into the dark.
Long ago, they say, the hero Hercules came to Spain and founded this city.
He was strong, but he was also a magician.
And under this hill he built an enchanted palace.
Inside, he left a secret.
Then he sealed the door with a lock.
Every king who ruled in Toledo after him came here and added one more lock.
Century after century, the door grew heavier with iron.
Until a king came who wanted to know.
What could be worth so many locks?
His name was Rodrigo, the last king of the Goths.
He believed there was treasure inside.
His lords begged him not to.
He broke the locks anyway, one after another, and walked in with a torch.
There was no gold.
There was only a chest.
And in the chest, a folded cloth.
He unfolded it.
Painted on it were horsemen he had never seen.
Strange faces.
Turbans on their heads.
Bows and lances in their hands.
And words beneath them.
Whoever opens this, men like these will take his kingdom.
Imagine him holding that cloth.
The torch shaking.
Every lock on the floor around him, broken by his own hand.
Within a year, the riders came.
They crossed the sea from Africa, and Rodrigo rode out to meet them, and he was never seen again.
The Goths' Spain was gone.
And why did they come?
Toledo has a second story for that.
Go down to the river, by the old bridge of San Martín, and you will find a ruined tower called the Bath of La Cava.
They say that from it, King Rodrigo watched a young girl bathing in the Tagus.
Florinda, the daughter of Count Julian.
He wanted her, and he took her.
Her father, who guarded the strait for the king, swore revenge.
And he opened the way across the sea for the invaders.
Now the history.
Rodrigo was real.
He really was the last Gothic king, and he really did lose his kingdom in battle in seven hundred and eleven.
The locked palace, the painted riders and Florinda are legend, written down by chroniclers long after.
And the cave itself?
Archaeologists say it is a Roman water tank, part of the system that fed the city.
The tower by the river is the stump of a medieval bridge.
Stand at the door and ask yourself the king's question.
Would you have opened it?
Next, the city of magicians, and the man who could make you live a whole life in an afternoon.
That is stop three.

tracks.room: Cueva de Hércules, Callejón de San Ginés, a few minutes from the cathedral

tracks.title: Stop 3. Toledo, school of magic: Don Illán and the Dean

sections.title: The city where they taught the dark arts

segments.text: Stop three.
This story has no single address.
The tour may tell it in a lane near the cathedral, or at the mouth of a cellar.
In the Middle Ages, across Europe, if a man said he had studied in Toledo, people crossed themselves.
The Toledan arts meant necromancy.
Students were said to learn it in caves beneath this city.
Here is the real root of the rumour.
After the Christian conquest, scholars came here from all over Europe.
Toledo had what no one else had: Arabic books on stars, medicine, mathematics, the Greek philosophers.
Christians, Jews and Muslims sat together and turned those books into Latin.
Astronomy looked like sorcery to people who could not read it.
So Toledo became the city of magicians.
A Spanish prince wrote the most famous of these stories seven centuries ago.
Listen.
A churchman, the Dean of Santiago, rides all the way to Toledo.
He has heard of a master of magic, Don Illán.
He begs to be taught.
Don Illán looks at him and says: men like you rise high, and then forget who helped them.
The Dean swears he will never forget.
So Don Illán agrees.
And he calls to his housekeeper.
Roast us two partridges for supper.
But do not cook them until I tell you.
Then, the lesson begins.
Messengers arrive.
The Dean's uncle, the archbishop, is dead.
The Dean is made bishop.
Then archbishop.
Then cardinal, in Rome.
Then Pope.
Years pass.
And at every step, Don Illán asks one small favour.
A post for his son.
And every time, the Dean says: not yet.
Next time.
At last, the Pope loses patience.
He calls his old teacher a heretic and a sorcerer, and threatens him with prison.
He will not even give him food for the road home.
Don Illán says quietly: then I will eat the partridges I ordered tonight.
And he calls out to his housekeeper.
And the Dean is sitting in a cellar in Toledo.
The same evening.
The same chair.
No Rome.
No crown.
The partridges are still raw.
It was all a spell, to see who he really was.
He was ashamed, says the book, and did not know what to say.
Don Illán sent him home without his lesson.
One more treasure belongs to this magic city.
They say the conquerors of Toledo found here the table of King Solomon, made of gold and jewels, and on it the secret name of God.
Two generals fought over it.
One broke off a leg to prove he found it first.
That is legend too.
Arab chroniclers wrote it down, and the table has never been found.
Every one of us has made the Dean's promise to someone.
Would you have kept it?
Next, down to a quiet street and a well with bitter water.
That is stop four.

tracks.room: Old town lanes; the guide may stop near the cathedral or a cellar

tracks.title: Stop 4. The Bitter Well: Raquel and Fernando

segments.text: Stop four.
The Bitter Well gives its name to a short street, Calle del Pozo Amargo, in the south of the old town, towards the river.
The well is in a tiny square, open to the street, so you can see it at any hour.
Look for a low stone ring, closed over, and a plaque on the wall.
Picture this lane when it was a garden behind a wall.
A well in the middle, with water so sweet the neighbours came for it.
And a girl who came to the well every evening.
Her name was Raquel.
She was the daughter of a Jewish family, the most beautiful girl in Toledo, they say.
And one evening, at the garden wall, a young Christian man named Fernando saw her.
And she saw him.
Nothing could have been more dangerous.
A Jewish girl and a Christian boy.
In this city, the three faiths lived side by side.
But they did not marry.
So what can two people do, when they cannot be seen together?
Hold on to that.
They meet at the well.
At night.
When the house is asleep, Raquel slips out to the garden, and Fernando climbs the wall.
They talk across the stone ring of the well, in whispers.
Every night.
For months.
And then her father finds out.
He does not shout.
He does not lock her in.
He does something worse.
He pays a man with a knife.
The next night, Fernando does not come.
Raquel waits by the well until dawn.
And the next night.
And the next.
She never learned what happened.
Or maybe she did.
She sat by that well and wept, night after night, and her tears fell into the water.
And the water turned bitter.
From then on, nobody could drink from it.
Some say that one night, looking down into the well, she saw his face in the water, and leaned in to reach him.
And did not come back up.
This is a legend, and it changes with every teller.
Even the father's name is different from one book to the next.
No record shows that Raquel or Fernando ever lived.
But the well is real.
A medieval well from a Jewish house.
Its stone ring was sealed in the nineteen sixties, and you can still see it here.
And the street still carries the name of bitter water.
Put your hand on the stone if you can.
Then ask: what would you have done, if you were Raquel, and he never came?
Next, out beyond the walls, to a Christ who came down from his cross to keep a promise.
That is stop five.

tracks.room: Calle del Pozo Amargo, a small lane in the south of the old town

tracks.title: Stop 5. Cristo de la Vega: the witness

sections.title: A promise at the foot of the cross

segments.text: Stop five.
The little church of the Cristo de la Vega stands outside the city walls, on the open plain below the north-west of the old town, a walk downhill from the Cambrón gate.
At night it is closed and the gates are locked.
If the tour comes here, you will see a white chapel behind a wall, with the dark city rising behind it.
Inside, out of sight tonight, is a carved Christ on the cross.
And something is wrong with him.
One arm is not nailed to the cross.
It hangs down, open, as if reaching for something.
Why?
Here is the story.
A Spanish poet, José Zorrilla, made it famous almost two hundred years ago, from an old Toledan tradition.
Inés de Vargas loves a young man, Diego Martínez.
He loves her, or says he does.
But he has to go to war in Flanders, to make his name.
Before he goes, she brings him here.
To this Christ.
And in front of the cross, Diego swears.
When I come back, I will marry you.
Three years pass.
No letter.
Then one day, soldiers come marching home through the city gate, and Inés runs to look.
And there he is.
Diego.
A captain now, made by the king.
She runs to him.
And he looks at her as if she were a stranger.
He says: I never promised you anything.
Inés goes to court.
The judge asks her: who saw this promise?
Was there a witness?
And she says: yes.
There was one.
The Christ of the Vega.
So the judge, and the lawyers, and the whole city, come down to this church.
And before the crucifix, the judge asks.
Do you swear that this man promised to marry this woman?
And a voice comes from the cross.
Yes.
I swear it.
And in the popular version, the Christ tears his right hand free of the nail, and lowers it, as if laying it on a book to take the oath.
And it never went back.
Zorrilla named his poem after an old Spanish saying.
A buen juez, mejor testigo.
To a good judge, a better witness.
And Diego and Inés?
Zorrilla does not give them a wedding.
Shaken by what they had seen, both turned away from the world, and spent their lives in religious houses.
This is legend.
Zorrilla's poem tells of a voice.
The lowered arm belongs to the popular telling, and the figure inside today is said to be a later replacement.
But think of her.
A woman with no proof, against a captain of the king.
And the one witness she had hung on a cross.
Next, a poet who walked these streets at night, and a soldier who kissed the wrong statue.
That is stop six.

tracks.room: Ermita del Cristo de la Vega, outside the walls on the plain below the north-west of the old town

tracks.title: Stop 6. Bécquer: The Kiss

sections.title: The poet in the dark streets

segments.text: Stop six.
This is a story by a poet, so it has no fixed stop.
But the poet does have an address.
Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer lived on Calle de San Ildefonso, a quiet street near the convent of San Clemente, in the north-west of the old town.
If the tour passes San Clemente, look at the church doorway.
Restorers cleaning it recently found a signature in pencil, thought to be his.
Bécquer was Spain's great romantic poet, a young man from Seville.
He loved Toledo at night.
He walked these lanes after dark, alone, sketching ruined churches with his brother, the painter Valeriano.
And out of those walks came his legends.
It is the time of the war against Napoleon.
French dragoons ride into Toledo, and there is no room left for them.
So they are put up in an old, half-ruined church.
Their horses stamp in the chapels.
Their captain is young, handsome and bored.
And one night, in the dark church, he finds something.
On a tomb, by the light of his lamp, kneel two figures carved in stone.
A knight in armour.
And beside him, his wife.
Doña Elvira.
Her hands joined in prayer.
And she is so beautiful that the captain cannot stop looking at her.
What happens when a living man falls in love with a woman of stone?
Hold on.
He comes back every night.
He tells his fellow officers he has found a lady in Toledo, the loveliest in the city, and they laugh at him.
So he invites them to supper.
In the church.
They light a fire with wood hacked from the carved choir stalls.
They drink.
They toast the lady.
And the captain shows them his lady, kneeling in stone.
The captain is drunk now.
He mocks the stone knight beside her, the husband who cannot defend her.
He raises his glass to him, and throws the wine in his face.
And then he says: I will kiss her.
He climbs up to the tomb.
He leans towards that cold stone face.
His lips come close.
And the officers hear a terrible sound.
A cry, and the crash of a body on stone.
They run to him.
The captain is lying at the foot of the tomb, blood running from his eyes, his nose, his mouth.
The stone knight has struck him down, with one terrible blow of his stone gauntlet.
The war was real.
French soldiers were quartered in Toledo's convents, and some did terrible damage.
But the church in the story, and the lovers on the tomb, are Bécquer's invention.
Walk on knowing this: a husband, carved in stone, still keeping watch over his wife.
Who would you trust to guard you, after you were gone?
Next, a short street, a clockmaker, and a man made of wood.
That is stop seven.

tracks.room: Old town lanes near the convent of San Clemente, north-west of the old town

tracks.title: Stop 7. Street of the Wooden Man: Juanelo's automaton

sections.title: A man who was not a man

segments.text: Stop seven.
The Calle del Hombre de Palo, the Street of the Wooden Man, is a short lane of about a hundred metres near the cathedral.
It is open at all hours.
Look for the street sign, and for a plaque that remembers who once walked here.
Picture this lane four and a half centuries ago.
Morning.
Shopkeepers opening their shutters.
And down the middle of the street, stiff and slow, walks a man made of wood.
He bows to the people he passes.
He carries a bowl.
At the archbishop's palace, they say, he stops, and someone fills the bowl with food.
Who made him?
And why would a machine beg for bread?
Hold on to that.
His maker was real.
Juanelo Turriano, an Italian clockmaker, the greatest of his age.
He built marvellous clocks for the emperor Charles the Fifth, and stayed in Spain to serve his son.
And here in Toledo he did something nobody thought possible.
The city sits high on its rock, and the river runs far below.
Water had to be carried up by donkey.
Juanelo built a vast machine of wood and metal that lifted the water of the Tagus all the way up to the Alcázar, the fortress at the top of the hill.
It was finished in fifteen sixty-nine.
But here is the turn.
He was owed money for it, and he was not paid in full.
The great engineer grew old and poor.
And so, the legend says, he built one last machine.
A wooden servant, to walk out each day and fetch what his master could no longer pay for.
The people of Toledo grew fond of it.
They dropped coins in its bowl.
And they named the street after it.
Juanelo, his water machine, and his money troubles are history.
He died in Toledo in fifteen eighty-five.
The walking wooden man is legend.
Some writers think there was only a wooden figure standing still, collecting alms.
Others believe he really did build moving figures, which would not be surprising for a man who made clocks that showed the heavens.
Even then, Toledans whispered that a man who could make water climb a mountain must be a magician.
One more street, if the tour takes you near Zocodover, the main square.
There is a narrow, dark alley there called the Alley of the Devil.
They say it is named for old stories of witchcraft and pacts with the devil.
And on windy nights, they say, you can still hear whispering between the walls.
That one, nobody has ever proved.
Listen anyway.
Think of the old man.
A genius, forgotten.
And his last invention is a servant who never leaves him.
What would you build, if you could not ask anyone for help?
One more story for the walk home.
That is stop eight.

tracks.room: Calle del Hombre de Palo, a short street near the cathedral

tracks.title: Stop 8. The Christ of the Skull: a walk home, and goodnight

segments.text: Stop eight, the last one.
Listen to this on the way back, in any dark lane.
Toledans place the story near Calle de las Bulas, in the south-west of the old town, where a small Christ once hung under an archway, lit by a little lamp, with a skull at his feet.
It is Bécquer again.
And it begins with a party.
The king is about to ride to war against the Moors.
On the last night, there is a great feast at the Alcázar.
And the most beautiful woman at court, Doña Inés, drops her glove.
A perfumed glove, with gold buttons.
Two knights reach for it at the same moment.
Two old friends, born in Toledo, who learned to fight side by side.
Now they are rivals for the same woman.
The king has to step between them.
So they agree to settle it that night.
With swords.
They walk through the sleeping city to the only light they can find.
The little lamp in front of the Christ of the Skull.
They draw.
And the moment their blades touch, the lamp goes out.
Total darkness.
They step apart.
And the lamp lights again, by itself.
They try again.
Steel touches steel.
Darkness.
They part.
Light.
And then a voice.
From somewhere in the dark lane.
Low, strange.
They cannot understand a single word.
But both men freeze, and their swords fall from their hands.
What does a man do, when heaven itself refuses to light his duel?
Hold on.
They make peace.
And together they walk to her house.
They are below her balcony as the sky turns grey.
And at dawn, a rope comes down from that balcony.
And down the rope climbs a man.
A third man.
And Doña Inés leans out to wave him goodbye.
The two knights look at each other.
And they burst out laughing.
Friends again.
The next day, as the army rides out, Doña Inés sees them laughing at her.
And one tear of spite rolls down her face.
That is a legend, by a poet.
Nobody fought here.
But Toledans still tell it, and it is a good one to carry home through dark streets.
So, Monica.
Tonight you have heard a horse kneel, a king break the locks, a well turn bitter, a crucifix speak, and a stone knight strike.
None of it is history.
All of it is Toledo.
If the Spanish tour carried you past these doors tonight, I hope you knew exactly where you were.
Tomorrow, the tracks take you back to these places by daylight, with the real stories behind the walls.
Walk slowly.
Watch the lamps.
And if one of them goes out as you pass, keep walking.
Goodnight.

tracks.room: Any dark lane on the way home; Toledans place it near Calle de las Bulas
